title: Simchat Torah: seven circles
hook: seven dancing circuits with the Torah scrolls

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shemini Atzeret, the eighth day of assembly. Your line was stay one more day. Today, the party that ends the season.

Picture a synagogue where nobody is sitting down. The ark is open and empty, because every scroll is out, in somebody's arms. A man in his eighties holds one, then hands it to a teenager. Children run between legs waving flags. Someone starts a song, the circle tightens, and the crowd goes around the reading table, sometimes spilling out the door and into the street. Then the music stops, the scrolls change hands, and it starts again. By the end of the night, people have gone around seven times, and almost nobody has kept count.
screen: `THE ARK IS EMPTY.` → `EVERY SCROLL IN SOMEONE'S ARMS.` → `AROUND AND AROUND.`

segments.voice: Simchat Torah means rejoicing of the Torah. In the Land of Israel it falls on Shemini Atzeret itself; outside Israel, where the festival has an extra day, it comes the day after. Either way it marks one thing: the yearly reading of the Torah is finished, and immediately begun again. The last words of Deuteronomy are read, about the great things Moses did, in the old Jewish translation, "in the sight of all Israel." Then, without a pause, Genesis: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." The person honored with the ending is called the bridegroom of the Torah; the one honored with the beginning, the bridegroom of Genesis. Today, in many communities, women are honored this way too. The dancing circuits are called hakafot, from a Hebrew root meaning to go around. You've met circuits this week: with the lulav on Sukkot, and seven on Hoshana Rabbah. Now the scroll replaces the palm branch, and dancing replaces pleas. The Bible says nothing about this day. The name Simchat Torah comes centuries after the Talmud, and the seven dancing hakafot are later still, spreading widely in the early modern period. It grew from the people up, not from a verse down. In many synagogues every child is called to the Torah together, under one large prayer shawl held up like a roof. And everyone, scholar or not, gets a turn to hold the scroll and dance.
screen: `THE LAST WORD, THEN THE FIRST.` · `BRIDEGROOMS OF THE TORAH.` · `HAKAFOT: GOING AROUND.` · `A CUSTOM FROM THE PEOPLE UP.` · then, large: `DANCE WITH THE SCROLL.`

segments.voice: Think of a book, a song or a teaching you love enough to carry around, and picture holding it in your arms. If you're somewhere you can, stand and turn one slow circle, or sway where you sit, the way your heart moves when something you love comes back around. Then rest.
Hakafot. Circuits, goings-around: seven dancing circles with the Torah scrolls on Simchat Torah. Today's word.
Your line: dance with the scroll. The last word leads straight back to the first. That's day six hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: On Simchat Torah, communities take every Torah scroll from the ark and dance seven hakafot around the reading table, then read the end of Deuteronomy and the start of Genesis; many call all the children up together under a large tallit.
